title: NumPy Quick Revision: Arrays, Broadcasting and Why Pandas Sits on Top
summary: Night-before revision notes on the NumPy ndarray, dtypes and shape, vectorised operations, broadcasting, boolean masks, the axis argument, views versus copies, and why pandas builds on NumPy.

chapters.title: ndarray, dtypes and shape: the mental model
points: ndarray = fixed-size, homogeneous block of contiguous memory plus metadata (dtype, shape, strides); every element has the same type, unlike a Python list
shape is a tuple of dimension lengths: np.zeros((2,3)).shape == (2,3); ndim = len(shape); size = product of shape
dtype sets bytes per element and behaviour: int64, float64, bool, and so on; check with a.dtype, convert with a.astype('float32') which returns a new array
Mixed inputs upcast to one dtype: np.array([1, 2.5, 'a']) becomes a string array; ints plus floats become float64
Gotcha: integer dtypes overflow silently (np.uint8(255)+1 wraps to 0), and reshape needs matching size: a.reshape(2,-1) lets NumPy infer one dimension

chapters.title: Vectorised operations and broadcasting rules
points: Vectorised = whole-array operations run in compiled C loops: a * 2 + b replaces a Python for-loop and is typically 10-100x faster
Ufuncs (np.add, np.sqrt, np.exp) apply elementwise; operators like +, *, ** map to them and * is elementwise, not matrix multiply (use @ or np.dot)
Broadcasting rule: compare shapes from the trailing dimension backwards; two dims are compatible if they are equal or one of them is 1; a missing leading dim counts as 1
Example: (3,1) + (1,4) gives (3,4), and (5,3) + (3,) gives (5,3); (3,) + (4,) raises ValueError: operands could not be broadcast together
Gotcha: a (n,) vector against an (n,1) column silently broadcasts to (n,n); fix the shape with a[:, None] or reshape(-1,1)

chapters.title: Boolean masks and the axis argument
points: Comparison makes a boolean mask of the same shape: mask = a > 5; indexing a[mask] returns a 1-D array of the True elements
Combine masks with & | ~ and parentheses, not and/or: a[(a > 2) & (a < 8)]; and/or raises ValueError on arrays
np.where(cond, x, y) picks x or y elementwise; np.where(cond) alone returns the indices of True; mask.sum() counts matches and mask.any()/all() test them
axis names the dimension that gets collapsed: for shape (rows, cols), a.sum(axis=0) gives one value per column, and a.sum(axis=1) gives one per row
axis=None (the default) reduces over everything to one scalar; keepdims=True keeps the reduced axis as size 1, so the result broadcasts straight back, e.g. a - a.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)

chapters.title: Views vs copies and why pandas builds on NumPy
points: Basic slicing (a[1:4], a[:, 0], a.T, a.reshape(...)) returns a view that shares memory, so writing to the slice changes the original
Boolean-mask and fancy (integer list) indexing return a copy: b = a[a > 5] never changes a; assigning a[a > 5] = 0 still writes into a
Check with np.shares_memory(a, b) or b.base is a; force independence with b = a[1:4].copy(), which is the standard fix for accidental mutation
Pandas Series and DataFrame columns are backed by NumPy arrays with a dtype, so they inherit vectorised ops, masks (df[df.x > 5]), the axis argument (df.sum(axis=1)) and broadcasting-style alignment
Pandas adds labelled index and columns, per-column dtypes, and NaN-aware missing-data handling; .to_numpy() exposes the array, which may or may not be a view, so copy before mutating

chapters.title: NumPy Cheat Sheet
points: Create: np.array(list), np.zeros(shape), np.ones(shape), np.arange(0,10,2), np.linspace(0,1,5); inspect with a.shape, a.dtype, a.ndim, a.size
Reshape and convert: a.reshape(r,-1), a.T, a.astype(float), a.ravel(), np.newaxis or a[:, None] to add an axis
Broadcast check: align shapes on the right, each pair must be equal or 1; use keepdims=True on reductions to keep shapes compatible
Mask and axis: a[(a>2)&(a<8)], np.where(c,x,y), a.sum(axis=0) is per column, a.sum(axis=1) is per row, a.mean(), a.max(), a.argmax()
Views vs copies: slices are views, masks and fancy indexing are copies, .copy() makes a safe duplicate; pandas wraps NumPy arrays, so df.to_numpy() and df.values bridge the two
